document.title: Cable from Ambassador Oakley, Amembassy Islamabad: "Subject: Ambassador Oakley's Meeting with General Beg"
document.authors: Ambassador Robert Oakley, U.S. Embassy Islamabad
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
document.note: Oakley meets Army Chief Gen. Mirza Aslam Beg after Zia's death. Beg claims India, the USSR and Afghanistan are destabilizing Pakistan, envisions a strategic consensus of Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, and says the resistance could choke Soviet withdrawal routes; Hekmatyar and Rabbani would not cede power.

events.description: Ambassador Oakley meets General Beg at GHQ.
President Zia's aircraft crashes; Beg suggests possible state-supported terrorism.
Assassination of TNFJ leader Arif Hussaini in Peshawar.
Beg addresses army officers in Rawalpindi on constitutional procedures.
Beg addressed Army officers in Rawalpindi stressing constitutional procedures.
Oakley and General Pfister met General Beg, discussing M1A1 tanks, AWACS deferral, pending requests (F-16s, TPQ-37 radars, C-NITE), Afghanistan strategy and Iraq.
Beg stated the mujahedin were paralyzing Soviet communications north of the Hindu Kush and could choke withdrawal routes.
Ambassador Oakley met General Beg at GHQ to discuss the political situation, strategic consensus, security assistance and Afghanistan.
Assassination of TNFJ leader Arif Hussein al-Hussaini in Peshawar in early August.
Soviet reoccupation of Kunduz and violations of Pakistani airspace described by Oakley as acts of desperation.
Beg said he would not stage a coup and would follow constitutional procedures after Zia's death.

key_claims: Beg claimed a 'triangular conspiracy' of Afghanistan, USSR and India was destabilizing Pakistan.
Beg asserted KHAD was behind the assassination of Shia leader Arif Hussaini, citing a high-ranking KHAD defector.
Beg suggested Zia's 17 August crash was possibly state-supported terrorism.
Beg said the resistance would negotiate with Kabul rather than seek Najib's collapse, and that Hekmatyar and Rabbani would not cede power to those who hadn't fought the Soviets.
Beg proposed a 'strategic consensus' of Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey; the embassy saw it as continuing Zia's quest for strategic depth against India.
